name: Crossing the river
statement: A swimmer moves at 1.6 m/s relative to the water. The river flows at 1.2 m/s. She points herself straight across a 40 m wide river. How far downstream, in meters, does she land?
solution: The two velocity components are independent. Crossing time is set by the perpendicular component alone: $t = 40/1.6 = 25$ s. In that time the current carries her $1.2 \times 25 = 30$ m downstream.

name: Aiming upstream
statement: Same swimmer (1.6 m/s in still water, 1.2 m/s current, 40 m river). Now she wants to land directly opposite her start. How long, in seconds, does the crossing take?
solution: To cancel the drift she aims upstream so that the upstream component equals the current: the across-stream speed becomes $\sqrt{1.6^2 - 1.2^2} = 1.058$ m/s. Then $t = 40/1.058 \approx 37.8$ s. Fighting the current costs her about 13 seconds.

name: Work at an angle
statement: A force $\vec F = (3, 4)$ N acts on a crate that slides along $\vec d = (4, 0)$ m. How much work does the force do, in joules?
solution: Work is the dot product: $W = F_x d_x + F_y d_y = 12 + 0 = 12$ J. Only the component along the motion contributes.

name: Stopping distance
statement: A train moving at 30 m/s brakes uniformly at 1.2 m/s². How far, in meters, does it travel before stopping?
solution: No time is mentioned, so use the time-free relation $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$. Setting $v = 0$: $\Delta x = v_0^2/2a = 900/2.4 = 375$ m.

name: Half-distance averages
statement: You drive the first half of a trip's distance at 40 mph and the second half at 60 mph. What is your average speed for the whole trip, in mph?
solution: Equal distances take unequal times, so the arithmetic mean is wrong. For each half of length $d$: $t = d/40 + d/60$. Then $\bar v = 2d/t = 48$ mph. This is the harmonic mean, always below the naive 50.

name: Dropped from a rising balloon
statement: A balloon rises at a steady 5 m/s. At a height of 60 m a sandbag is released. Using $g = 10$ m/s², how long, in seconds, until the bag hits the ground?
solution: The bag leaves with the balloon's velocity, $+5$ m/s upward. Taking up as positive with the ground at $y = -60$: $-60 = 5t - 5t^2$. So $t^2 - t - 12 = 0$, giving $t = 4$ s. Forgetting the initial upward velocity gives 3.46 s, which is the classic wrong answer.

name: Off the cliff
statement: A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from a cliff 45 m high. Using $g = 10$ m/s², how far from the base of the cliff does it land, in meters?
solution: Vertical motion sets the clock: $t = \sqrt{2h/g} = 3$ s. Horizontal motion is uniform: $x = 15 \times 3 = 45$ m. The two directions never mix.

name: The other angle
statement: A projectile launched at 25° covers a certain range on level ground. What other launch angle, in degrees, gives the same range at the same speed?
solution: Range goes as $\sin 2\theta$, and $\sin(180° - x) = \sin x$. So $2\theta_2 = 180° - 50°$, giving $\theta_2 = 65°$. Complementary angles always share a range.

name: Down the slope
statement: A ball is launched horizontally at 8 m/s from the top of a 30° incline and lands on the slope. Using $g = 10$ m/s², how far along the incline, in meters, does it land?
solution: Let the landing point be a distance $L$ down the slope, so $x = L\cos30°$ and $y = L\sin30°$. From $x = 8t$ and $y = 5t^2$: $L\sin30° = 5(L\cos30°/8)^2$. Solving, $L = 8\sin30°\cdot 64/(5\cdot 64 \cos^2 30°)$ ... more directly $t = 2v\tan\theta/g = 0.924$ s, $x = 7.39$ m, $L = x/\cos30° = 8.87$ m.

name: Atwood machine
statement: A 3 kg block and a 2 kg block hang from a light string over a frictionless pulley. Using $g = 10$ m/s², what is the magnitude of their acceleration, in m/s²?
solution: Write $\sum F = ma$ for each mass with the same tension and the same acceleration magnitude, then add the equations to eliminate $T$: $a = (m_1 - m_2)g/(m_1 + m_2) = 10/5 = 2$ m/s².

name: Held on a frictionless slope
statement: A 2 kg block sits on a frictionless 40° incline, held in place by a purely horizontal force. Using $g = 10$ m/s², what is the normal force, in newtons?
solution: Resolve along and perpendicular to the incline. Equilibrium along the slope gives $F = mg\tan\theta$; perpendicular gives $N = mg/\cos\theta = 20/\cos40° = 26.1$ N. The reflex answer $mg\cos\theta$ assumes the applied force is along the slope, which it is not.

name: Block on a block
statement: A 1 kg block rests on a 4 kg block on a frictionless floor. The coefficient of static friction between them is 0.30. Using $g = 10$ m/s², what is the largest horizontal force, in newtons, that can be applied to the bottom block without the top one slipping?
solution: The only horizontal force on the top block is friction, so its maximum acceleration is $a = \mu g = 3$ m/s². Both blocks must share that acceleration, so $F = (m_1+m_2)a = 5 \times 3 = 15$ N.

name: Bullet in a block
statement: A 10 g bullet moving at 400 m/s embeds itself in a stationary 1.99 kg block on a frictionless surface. What is the speed of the combined object afterward, in m/s?
solution: Sticking together means perfectly inelastic: momentum is conserved, kinetic energy is not. $v = m_b v_b/(m_b + M) = 4/2 = 2$ m/s. Kinetic energy falls from 800 J to 4 J; the missing 796 J went into heat and deformation.

name: Minimum loop height
statement: A cart starts from rest at height $h$ and runs without friction into a vertical loop of radius 2 m. Using $g = 10$ m/s², what is the minimum $h$, in meters, for the cart to keep contact at the top?
solution: At the critical speed gravity alone supplies the centripetal force at the top: $v^2 = gr$. Energy conservation to a height $2r$: $gh = 2gr + \tfrac12 gr$, so $h = 2.5r = 5$ m.

name: Explosion on the way up
statement: A 4 kg projectile at the top of its arc, moving horizontally at 30 m/s, explodes into two equal pieces. One piece falls straight down (zero horizontal velocity). What is the horizontal speed of the other piece, in m/s?
solution: The explosion is internal, so horizontal momentum is conserved: $4(30) = 2(0) + 2v$, giving $v = 60$ m/s. The center of mass continues on the original parabola regardless of the explosion.

name: Banked curve
statement: A curve of radius 50 m is banked so that a car needs no friction at 20 m/s. Using $g = 10$ m/s², what is the banking angle, in degrees?
solution: With no friction the horizontal component of the normal force supplies the centripetal force: $\tan\theta = v^2/(gr) = 400/500 = 0.8$, so $\theta = 38.7°$. Notice the mass cancels.

name: Orbit period ratio
statement: Satellite B orbits at four times the radius of satellite A. By what factor is B's period longer than A's?
solution: Kepler's third law: $T^2 \propto r^3$, so $T_B/T_A = 4^{3/2} = 8$.

name: Quadrupled mass
statement: A mass on a spring oscillates with a period of 2.0 s. The mass is quadrupled. What is the new period, in seconds?
solution: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$, so the period scales as $\sqrt{m}$: quadrupling the mass doubles the period to 4.0 s. Amplitude is irrelevant, which is the defining feature of SHM.

name: Pendulum on Mars
statement: A pendulum has a period of 2.0 s on Earth ($g = 9.8$ m/s²). What is its period, in seconds, on Mars where $g = 3.7$ m/s²?
solution: $T \propto 1/\sqrt{g}$, so $T_{Mars} = 2.0\sqrt{9.8/3.7} = 3.26$ s. Weaker gravity means a slower swing.

name: Two springs in series
statement: A 2 kg mass hangs from two springs connected end to end, each with $k = 400$ N/m. What is the oscillation frequency, in Hz?
solution: Springs in series share the load but their extensions add, so $1/k_{eff} = 1/400 + 1/400$ and $k_{eff} = 200$ N/m. Then $f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{200/2} = 1.59$ Hz. In parallel you would instead add the constants.

name: Rolling race
statement: A solid sphere ($I = \tfrac25 mr^2$) rolls without slipping from rest down a 2 m high ramp. Using $g = 10$ m/s², what is its speed at the bottom, in m/s?
solution: Energy splits between translation and rotation: $mgh = \tfrac12 mv^2(1 + 2/5)$. So $v = \sqrt{10gh/7} = \sqrt{200/7} = 5.35$ m/s. A sliding block would reach 6.32 m/s; the sphere is slower because some energy goes into spin.

name: Falling rod
statement: A uniform rod of length 1.2 m is held vertically on a frictionless pivot at its base and released. Using $g = 10$ m/s², what is the speed of its tip when it hits the ground, in m/s?
solution: The center of mass falls $L/2$: $mgL/2 = \tfrac12 I\omega^2$ with $I = mL^2/3$. So $\omega = \sqrt{3g/L}$ and the tip moves at $v = \omega L = \sqrt{3gL} = 6.0$ m/s.

name: Inside a uniform sphere
statement: A solid insulating sphere of radius 0.2 m carries charge spread uniformly through its volume. The field at the surface is 900 N/C. What is the field, in N/C, at 0.1 m from the center?
solution: Inside, the enclosed charge grows as $r^3$ while the Gaussian area grows as $r^2$, so the field is linear in $r$: $E = E_{surf}(r/R) = 900 \times 0.5 = 450$ N/C.

name: Shielded, or not
statement: A $+3\ \mu$C point charge sits at the center of an uncharged conducting shell. What is the total charge, in microcoulombs, on the shell's outer surface?
solution: Induction puts $-3\ \mu$C on the inner surface so the conductor's interior field vanishes. The shell is neutral overall, so $+3\ \mu$C appears on the outside. Conductors shield their insides, not their outsides.

name: Resistor cube
statement: Twelve 1 Ω resistors form the edges of a cube. What is the resistance, in ohms, between two opposite corners?
solution: By symmetry the current splits 3-way, then 6-way, then 3-way: $R = R(1/3 + 1/6 + 1/3) = 5/6 = 0.833$ Ω. Symmetry lets you merge equipotential nodes instead of solving twelve loop equations.

name: RC time constant
statement: A 10 μF capacitor charges through a 50 kΩ resistor from a 12 V source. How long, in seconds, until the capacitor reaches 6 V?
solution: $V = V_0(1 - e^{-t/RC})$ with $RC = 0.5$ s. Half charge gives $t = RC\ln 2 = 0.347$ s.

name: Speed of a gas molecule
statement: What is the rms speed, in m/s, of a nitrogen molecule (28 g/mol) at 300 K? Use $R = 8.31$ J/mol·K.
solution: $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M} = \sqrt{3(8.31)(300)/0.028} = 517$ m/s. Equipartition puts $\tfrac32 k_BT$ into each molecule's translation.

name: Carnot ceiling
statement: An engine runs between 600 K and 300 K. What is the maximum possible efficiency, as a percentage?
solution: $\eta_{max} = 1 - T_C/T_H = 1 - 0.5 = 50\%$. Any real engine between these reservoirs does worse; claiming better violates the second law.

name: Beat frequency
statement: Two tuning forks at 440 Hz and 444 Hz sound together. What is the beat frequency, in Hz?
solution: Beats occur at the difference frequency: $|444 - 440| = 4$ Hz, heard as four loudness swells per second.

name: Doppler approach
statement: An ambulance siren emits 800 Hz while approaching you at 30 m/s. With sound at 340 m/s, what frequency, in Hz, do you hear?
solution: Moving source, stationary observer: $f' = f\,v/(v - v_s) = 800(340/310) = 877$ Hz. The wavefronts pile up ahead of the source.

name: Thin lens image
statement: An object sits 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. How far, in centimeters, is the image from the lens?
solution: $1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$ gives $1/d_i = 1/20 - 1/30 = 1/60$, so $d_i = 60$ cm. Positive means a real image on the far side.

name: Relativistic time dilation
statement: A muon lives 2.2 μs at rest. Traveling at 0.99c, how long, in microseconds, does it live in the lab frame?
solution: $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - 0.99^2} = 7.09$, so the lab lifetime is $7.09 \times 2.2 = 15.6$ μs. This is why cosmic-ray muons reach the ground.

name: Photoelectric threshold
statement: A metal has a work function of 2.3 eV. What is the longest wavelength of light, in nanometers, that still ejects electrons?
solution: At threshold the photon energy equals the work function: $\lambda = hc/\phi = 1240\ \text{eV·nm}/2.3\ \text{eV} = 539$ nm. Longer wavelengths eject nothing no matter how intense.
